items.followUp: What is hydrogen bonding? Name one substance in which it occurs.

rubric.why: Checks that the student identifies the hydrogen atom and the highly electronegative atom involved.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O or N.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying hydrogen bonded to at least one of F, O or N.

rubric.why: Checks that the student explains hydrogen bonding as an attraction between molecules.
rubric.description: Identifies the attraction between the hydrogen and an electronegative atom of another molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the intermolecular attraction.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and an electronegative atom of another molecule.

items.followUp: State the three ways atoms can achieve a stable outer electron shell.

rubric.why: Checks that the student states both electron loss and electron gain as ways of achieving an octet.
rubric.description: States that an atom can lose electrons and gain electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both losing and gaining electrons.

rubric.why: Checks that the student states electron sharing as the third way of achieving an octet.
rubric.description: States that an atom can share electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating sharing electrons.

modelAnswer: An atom can accommodate eight electrons in its valence shell by losing electrons, gaining electrons or sharing electrons.

items.followUp: Define crystalline solids and give one example.

accept: not arranged in a regular pattern
rubric.why: Checks the defining arrangement of particles in an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: States that the particles in an amorphous solid are not arranged in a regular pattern.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the irregular arrangement of particles.

rubric.why: Checks that the student gives a valid example of an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: Gives one example, such as glass, plastic or rubber.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.
Glass is an example of an amorphous solid.

items.followUp: How does ionization energy change as electropositivity increases?

rubric.why: Checks the direction of the relationship between electropositivity and ionization energy.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the inverse relationship.

accept: less energy to remove an electron
rubric.why: Checks the chemical explanation for the inverse relationship.
rubric.description: Explains that electropositive atoms lose electrons readily and therefore have low ionization energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that electron removal is easier or requires less energy.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
An electropositive atom loses an electron readily, so its ionization energy is low.

items.followUp: Explain why water dissolves many ionic compounds, and give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of the principle that like substances dissolve like substances.
rubric.description: States that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct principle.

rubric.why: Checks that the student illustrates the principle with a valid solute-solvent pair.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example, such as sodium chloride dissolving in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
For example, sodium chloride dissolves in water.
